title: The Coil
author: Alexandre Dias
excerpt: She noticed the mark on the seventh morning. A faint spiral at the base of her throat, no larger than a fingernail clipping. She rubbed at it and thought nothing of it. She was, in every way she could measure, an unremarkable woman — and had, for forty-one years, been very good at it.

chapters.title: The Mark
chapters.body:
She noticed the mark on the seventh morning.

It was above her collarbone, just to the left of the notch at the base of her throat, in the small hollow where her mother used to press a fingertip when she was a child and say *there you are, my Isolde, my only one.* A faint spiral, the size of a fingernail clipping, drawn in a shade barely darker than her skin. She saw it in the mirror while brushing her teeth and stopped brushing.

She stood with the toothbrush in her mouth and looked.

The mark was not a bruise. She would have known a bruise. It was not a mole; her skin had no moles. It was not the impression a strap or a chain might leave, and there was nothing in her wardrobe that could have made a spiral like that, so precise, so evenly curled from center to edge.

She rinsed her mouth. She put on her glasses. She looked again, closer, until her breath fogged the glass.

The spiral had four turns. It coiled inward from the outside, tightening, disappearing into a single dark point at its center. It did not look drawn. It did not look pressed. It looked, she thought — and hated the thought as soon as she had it — *grown.*

She rubbed at it with her thumb. It did not lift, did not smudge, did not warm. She rubbed harder. When she took her thumb away her skin was pink from the friction, but the spiral was untouched, calm at its center, waiting.

She was forty-one years old. She lived alone in the flat above the bookshop where she worked. She had a mother who called on Sundays and a sister who did not. She had never been married and did not want to be. She had been, at various points in her life, in love, out of love, tired, and content, sometimes all in the same week. She had rules about her body: no piercings, no tattoos, no dyes, no fillers. She kept her nails short. She kept her hair to her shoulders. She had, since her twenties, insisted upon being unremarkable, and had done well at it.

The spiral was not a remarkable thing. It was small. It was not painful. But it was, she understood at once, hers now — not something done to her, but something belonging to her, in the way her fingernails belonged to her and could not be given away.

She rubbed at it a third time, and then she covered it with her hand, and then she went to work.

—

The shop opened at ten. She unlocked the door at nine-forty-two, as she always did, and turned on the lamps in the front window, and set out the small blackboard on the pavement with the day's specials written in her careful, backward-leaning script. She made tea. She counted the till. She did all of the things she did every morning and found that she was doing them, this morning, with only about half of herself, and that the other half of herself was standing in the bathroom in front of the mirror, watching a small spiral not move.

At eleven, Mrs. Halloran came in for her weekly Trollope. At eleven-thirty, a man Isolde had never seen bought three postcards and asked if she had anything by Ligotti. She said she did, in the back, on the shelf beside the Aickman. He said thank you and went to look and did not come out for a long time. Sometime after that she heard him leave. He had not, she noticed later, bought a Ligotti.

At one o'clock she closed the shop for lunch, went upstairs, and looked in the mirror again.

The spiral was still there. She had known it would be. She had known, also, though she could not have said how she knew, that it would be a little larger. It was.

It was now the size of a small coin, and the tightness of its center had loosened by perhaps a quarter of a turn, so that where before there had been a solid dark point, there was now a smaller spiral, curled inside the first, spiraling on into detail she could not resolve without a magnifying glass. She fetched a magnifying glass from the shop. She looked.

Inside the smaller spiral was a smaller one still.

She turned off the bathroom light. She turned it back on. She looked again. The spiral did not respond to light or its absence. It sat quietly on her skin, a small quiet aperture into something she could not see, and she felt — this was the moment, she would remember later, when she began to feel — that if she were to look long enough into the center, something in the center would look back.

She did not look long enough.

She went downstairs and opened the shop and served a woman who wanted a book about mushrooms, and by the time the woman had gone Isolde had convinced herself that she would call her doctor in the morning, and that until then she would not think about it.

She thought about it all afternoon.

—

At six she closed the shop and walked to the chemist's on the corner and bought a tube of concealer two shades too pale for her skin. The girl at the till was seventeen and had a ring in her nose. She smiled at Isolde as though selling concealer to a woman in her forties were a small, private mercy. Isolde did not smile back.

At home she washed her face and applied the concealer over the spiral. It disappeared. She looked at herself in the mirror and could not see the mark at all, only her own skin, gone slightly paler in one small place, like a patch of frost.

She was so grateful she felt her eyes sting.

She made herself dinner. She ate at the kitchen table with a book open beside her plate, though she did not read it. She washed the dishes. She turned off the lights. She lay in bed and put her hand over the place where the spiral was, and felt her own pulse in her throat, steady and stupid and alive, and she said aloud to the dark, *it is nothing,* and the dark did not answer, because the dark, unlike the spiral, was not there.

—

She slept, and dreamed of nothing, and woke at four in the morning with her heart pounding and a certainty in her chest that she could not name.

She got up. She went to the bathroom. She turned on the light and stood before the mirror and washed the concealer off with a hot flannel, slowly, because she was afraid.

The spiral had moved.

It was no longer at the base of her throat. It was two inches lower, and one inch further to the left, as if it had slid across her skin while she slept. She stared at it. The old place, where it had been that morning, was smooth and empty and pale. The new place, where it was now, held the spiral just as it had been at lunchtime — the size of a coin, four visible turns, smaller spirals nested within.

She touched the old place with her fingertips. Nothing there. She touched the new place. The spiral, under her fingertip, was cool.

She was not, she noted with distant surprise, screaming.

She sat down on the edge of the bath. She put her head between her knees and breathed until the small black stars faded from her vision. When she stood up again she was calmer than she had any right to be. Some part of her, she recognized, had already begun to accept the situation, in the way a body sometimes accepted a wound before the mind had caught up to it, in the way one might accept, upon waking in a strange bed, that the day would proceed regardless.

She looked at the mirror again. The spiral looked back.

She thought: *I have to tell someone.*

She thought: *I have no one to tell.*

She thought, with a cold clarity that surprised her: *I don't want to.*

She realized then, standing barefoot on the cold tile at four in the morning, that this last thought was the true thing, and the previous two had been arranged to disguise it. She did not want to tell anyone. She did not want anyone to see. The mark was hers. It had chosen her, or grown from her, or come to her in her sleep out of some dark cabinet in the world, and it was hers, and she did not want to share it.

She looked at the small spiral. The small spiral looked at her, or seemed to. She thought — and this was the thought she would remember, later, when she tried to trace back the exact hour at which she had lost herself — she thought:

*It is beautiful.*

She turned off the light and went back to bed.

chapters.title: The Second Turn
chapters.body:
She kept a diary now.

She had never kept a diary in her life. She was not the sort of woman who kept diaries; she considered the practice slightly indecent, an admission that one's inner life was interesting enough to be recorded, and she had spent decades cultivating the belief that hers was not. But on the morning after the spiral moved, she took a notebook from the stock cupboard in the shop — a plain black notebook, one of the ones she sold to students at the college — and she began, in her small backward hand, to record.

*Day one,* she wrote. *Base of throat, left side. Size of a fingernail clipping. Four turns visible.*

*Day two, morning: unchanged from evening. Day two, midday: two inches lower, further left. Now the size of a coin.*

*Day three: another inch lower. On the swell of the breast now. Six turns visible when I look with the glass. It is warmer than the skin around it, by perhaps a degree. Not painful.*

She kept the notebook in the drawer of her bedside table, beneath a copy of *The Duino Elegies* she had not opened in ten years. She wrote in it every morning and every evening, and sometimes at lunch, and once in the middle of the night when she woke and found the spiral had crossed the line of her sternum in her sleep and was now, faintly and irrefutably, on the right side of her chest instead of the left.

She was, she realized, mapping a country.

—

She did not call the doctor.

She had meant to, on the second morning, and had picked up the phone, and had dialed the first six digits of the surgery's number before she stopped. She could not think what she would say. She did not know how to describe the mark in a way that would produce, in the doctor, the correct kind of alarm — the practical, professional kind, the kind that led to referrals and biopsies and pale rooms with fluorescent lighting. She could only imagine describing it in the wrong way, the true way, and being sent to a different sort of doctor entirely, one who did not deal with skin at all.

She put the phone down.

She thought about this, later, and did not like what she thought.

The truth, she wrote in the notebook on day four, was that she did not want the mark to be a medical thing. She did not want it to be a symptom of some illness that could be named and grouped with other illnesses, filed in a category with strangers who had the same illness and knew, therefore, precisely what she was going through. She did not want to be common. She did not want to be sympathized with. She did not want anyone else to have anything like it.

*I want it to be mine,* she wrote, and then she closed the notebook and did not write in it again for a day.

—

On day five she began to hear something.

It was not a sound, exactly. It was more like the sensation of a sound she could not quite catch, in the way one sometimes almost recognizes a piece of music heard through a wall two rooms away. It came in the small hours, when she lay very still in bed, and it seemed to come from the place where the spiral was. She would put her hand there and hold very still, and something in her chest would seem to be turning, very slowly, as though something wound like a small watch spring were unwinding at the pace of an hour hand.

She told no one. Whom would she have told?

—

On day six she took her clothes off in front of the mirror for the first time since childhood without immediately looking away.

She was, she saw, thinner. She had not been eating well. Her ribs made shadows she did not remember. Her hips, at forty-one, had begun to look a little bit like her mother's hips, and this ordinarily would have upset her, but tonight she found she did not care. She was looking for the spiral.

The spiral was on her sternum, at the fixed and central place where a heart, in a child's drawing, might be. It was the size of a saucer. It had, when she counted, eleven visible turns; there were more within, but her eyes could not resolve them without the glass. It was the color of old iron.

She looked at it for a long time.

She looked at her body around it, and understood, with a strange dispassion, that her body was changing to accommodate it. The skin over her breastbone was thinner than it should have been, more translucent, and she thought she could see, faintly, a shadow beneath it — as if the spiral did not lie on her skin but *in* her, at some shallow depth, and had already begun to burrow.

She thought: *I should be afraid.*

She was not. She had not been for days. What she was, instead, was a woman who had been given a thing very few people were ever given, and who was watching herself become the person who had been given it.

She raised her hand to her chest and laid the flat of her palm on the spiral. It was warm. Under her palm she could feel, or imagined she could feel, the slow turning, the patient watchmaker's motion, some very small mechanism keeping time. She closed her eyes.

She thought, very clearly: *If I take my hand away, will I still hear it?*

She took her hand away. She still heard it.

She began to laugh. She did not know why she was laughing. She laughed in the small tiled bathroom, naked, with a spiral on her chest, and heard herself laughing, and thought: *this is the sound of my voice, and I do not recognize it,* and laughed harder.

—

At the shop the next day she was — she must have been — normal. She sold books. She made change. She spoke to the couriers. Mrs. Halloran came in for her Trollope and said, at the till, in her wide voice, *Isolde dear, you look wonderful,* and Isolde said thank you, and Mrs. Halloran said, *no, but really — you're glowing.*

Isolde said thank you again and did not correct her.

She was, she saw when Mrs. Halloran had gone, glowing. She had gone to the small mirror in the back room and looked at her face, and her face was the face of a woman in love, or a woman on the second glass of wine, or a woman who had been told a secret worth keeping. Her cheeks were flushed. Her eyes were bright. She did not look like a sick person.

She looked, for the first time she could remember, *interesting.*

—

That evening she went home and stood in front of the mirror again, and she saw that the spiral had grown up her throat.

Not moved. *Grown.* One of the small spirals nested inside the large one had extended a fine curling line, delicate as a hair, and the line had risen from her sternum, up along the pale channel of her throat, and had begun — very finely, very lightly — to loop around the base of her jaw. She could see it now, when she turned her head. She could feel it, when she swallowed, as a small cool pressure against the tendons of her neck.

She thought, *tomorrow it will be on my face.*

She was correct.

—

She stopped going to the shop on day nine.

She left a note on the door — *closed for personal reasons, apologies* — and she disconnected the telephone, and she drew the curtains in the upstairs flat, and she sat down at her kitchen table with the notebook and a cup of tea, and she wrote:

*I do not think I am ill.*

She sat and thought about this.

*I do not think anything is wrong with me. I feel better than I have felt in years. I sleep well. I dream of nothing. My skin is warm. My hair is thicker. My eyes see more clearly than they have since I was a girl. If a doctor examined me now, I would pass every test. My blood pressure is low. My heart is strong. I am, by every measure I can think of, healthier than I was a week ago.*

*I only look wrong.*

She stopped and drank some tea and continued.

*If I go to a doctor I will be told this is a delusion. If I go to a priest I will be told it is a possession. If I go to my sister I will be told it is a nervous breakdown, and she will call our mother, and our mother will come, and I will have to look our mother in the eye. If I go to anyone at all I will be looked at, and touched, and photographed, and I will not be allowed to keep it.*

*I want to keep it.*

She looked at what she had written. She read it again. She thought: *this is the most honest sentence I have ever put on paper.*

She thought: *I am forty-one years old and I have never wanted anything the way I want this.*

She wrote, then, one more line, and then she closed the notebook, and she did not open it again until the last night.

*I want to know what it is.*

chapters.title: The Center
chapters.body:
The knock at the door came on the twelfth night.

She was sitting in the dark. She had been sitting in the dark for some time — she did not know how long — with her palms flat on the kitchen table and her eyes closed, listening. The turning inside her had grown louder. She could hear it now not as a suggestion of sound but as a real one, a slow soft grinding at the very edge of hearing, like a stone wheel deep beneath a mill. She had been listening to it for hours. It was, she had begun to think, saying something.

The knock came three times, and then stopped, and then came again, gentle but insistent.

She did not move.

The knock came a third time, and a voice she knew said, *Isolde. Isolde, please.*

She opened her eyes.

—

It was her sister. Of course it was her sister. There was no one else it could have been, at the door of her flat in the dark, at whatever hour it was, calling her name.

Isolde stood up slowly. Her knees were stiff; she had been sitting a long time. She walked into the hallway. She did not turn on the light. She stood on her side of the door and put her hand on the wood and listened.

*Isolde,* her sister said. *I know you're in there. Mum called me. She's been trying to reach you for four days.*

Four days. Isolde tried to remember four days. She could not.

*She's frightened,* her sister said. *I'm frightened. Please open the door.*

Isolde thought: *if I open the door, she will see.*

She thought: *if I open the door, this will end.*

She stood a long time with her hand on the wood.

*Isolde,* her sister said, softer now, closer to the door on her side, so that their two hands were separated by only the thickness of a single plank of pine and eighty centimeters of grain. *Please. I don't know what to do.*

Isolde opened the door.

—

Her sister looked at her.

Her sister did not scream. Her sister did not make any sound at all. Her sister looked at her, and Isolde watched her sister's face go through a sequence of small precise adjustments — the eyes wide, then narrow, then wide again, the mouth opening and closing without opening, the color leaving the cheeks and then, slowly, coming back — and Isolde understood that her sister, who had known her for thirty-eight years, was trying very hard not to appear to be seeing what she was seeing.

*Come in,* Isolde said. Her voice was strange in her own ears. She had not used it in some time.

Her sister came in. Her sister set down her bag on the small table in the hallway. Her sister took off her coat and hung it on the hook. Her sister did all of the small ordinary things one does upon arriving at a familiar house, and Isolde watched her do them, and understood that her sister was performing these small rituals as a means of not looking at her face.

—

They sat in the kitchen. Isolde turned on the light. Her sister did not flinch, but her eyes moved involuntarily, and Isolde saw them move, and knew what they were tracking. The spiral was, now, over her entire chest, and up her throat, and across her left cheek, and around her left eye. It had not stopped growing. It had, in the last day, begun to send fine tendrils down her arms. Her sister could see them now, at the wrists, where they had crept out from under her sleeves.

Her sister said, *Isolde. What have you done.*

Isolde said, *nothing. This is what happened.*

Her sister said, *when.*

Isolde said, *twelve days ago.*

Her sister closed her eyes.

—

She had brought a doctor. She had not said so at the door, but the doctor was in a car outside. Her sister explained this, sitting with her hands folded on the kitchen table, not looking at Isolde's face. The doctor was a friend. The doctor could be discreet. The doctor could come inside if Isolde wanted, or if Isolde did not want, could be sent away, and they would find another way.

Isolde said, *there is no other way.*

Her sister said, *what do you mean.*

Isolde said, *I mean I am not going to a hospital. I mean I am not going to be examined. I mean I am not going to be photographed, or biopsied, or asked when the symptoms began, or given anything to slow it down, or asked, at any point, whether I would like to have it removed. I am not going to any of that. I am not.*

Her sister said, softer, *Isolde.*

Isolde said, *don't.*

—

Her sister went home in the early hours of the morning.

She had cried. She had begged. She had, at one point, tried to touch Isolde's face, and Isolde had let her, and her sister had felt with her fingertips the fine cool curling lines and had drawn her hand back as if from something too hot. She had asked how it did not hurt. Isolde had said it did not hurt.

She had asked, at last, what Isolde wanted her to do.

Isolde had said: *tell Mum I love her. Tell her I am not in pain. Tell her I am not frightened. Tell her not to come.*

Her sister had said, *she is going to come.*

Isolde had said, *tell her not to. Please.*

She did not know if her sister would tell her. She did not know if her mother would come. She did not, when the door had closed and she stood alone again in her hallway, know very much about anything at all.

She did know one thing.

She knew, standing in her hallway with the sound of her sister's footsteps going away down the stairs and the fine slow turning in her chest louder now than it had ever been, that the mark had almost finished.

She knew this the way one knows the last minutes of a piece of music.

—

She went into the bathroom.

She turned on the light. She took off the loose shirt she had been wearing. She stood in front of the mirror, and she looked, and she saw.

The spiral had reached her navel, now, and down the tops of her thighs. It had covered both of her arms to the elbow. It had crossed her face entirely, both cheeks, the bridge of her nose, the delicate skin under her eyes, up into her hairline. Her hair, at the temples, was beginning to curl in the same pattern. She did not know how this was possible. She did not need to know.

She looked at herself.

She thought: *I am not a person any longer. I am a diagram.*

She thought: *I am not a diagram. I am a page.*

She thought: *I am not a page. I am the writing on the page.*

She thought: *I do not know what is written.*

And then, very quietly, in the small tiled bathroom that had once been a place where she had brushed her teeth and rinsed her face and looked at herself as an unremarkable woman with unremarkable rules, she heard the turning stop.

It stopped between one moment and the next. The slow grinding at the edge of hearing, which she had been listening to for days, ceased. In its place was a silence so complete she thought for a moment she had gone deaf.

She had not. Somewhere in the flat, the fridge was humming. Somewhere outside, a car was passing. The world was still making the sounds the world makes.

But inside her, the turning had stopped.

She stood very still.

She waited.

—

She saw it, then, in the mirror. She saw it very clearly.

The spiral over her sternum, the great one, the mother spiral, the one from which all the others had grown — its center, which had once been a single dark point the size of a pinhead, was open.

It was open the way a small door in a wall is open. It was a black aperture the size of her thumbnail, and it did not reflect the bathroom light. It was black in a way she had never seen black — a black that did not have any surface to it, a black that receded.

She leaned closer to the mirror.

She could see, in the aperture, that something was inside.

She could not, at first, resolve what it was. It was too small, and it was too far. She had the impression of curves. She had the impression of turning. She had the impression, in some fainter and more terrible way, of *waiting.*

She thought: *it has been waiting for me.*

She thought: *it has always been waiting for me.*

She thought — and this was a thought so old it seemed to arrive from a place before language — *hello.*

—

The thing in the center of the spiral did not answer.

It did not, in any way she could have named, look at her.

But she felt it, unmistakably and without alarm, notice her.

She felt it notice her the way a very old thing, disturbed after a long sleep, notices the disturbance — not with recognition, not with welcome, but with a slow patient turning-toward. She felt it turning toward her now, from wherever it was, from some depth in her chest that was not the depth of her chest at all, but the depth of some other room, some other body, some other world nested in hers the way her spirals were nested in themselves.

She felt it come to the door.

She felt it look out.

She thought: *I did not know I was the door.*

—

She did not scream. She had not screamed in a long time. She would not scream now.

She stood in front of the mirror and watched her own face — spiraled, patient, no longer entirely hers — and she watched the small dark aperture at the center of her chest, and she waited.

She waited a long time.

Slowly, very slowly, she raised her hand. She placed her palm flat against the mirror, over the reflection of her own chest, over the small dark opening. Her palm was warm against the cold glass.

She thought: *I am going in.*

She did not know if she meant it as a statement or a plea.

She thought: *do you want me?*

The thing in the center did not answer. But she felt it, then, do the smallest thing. She felt it — how to describe it — *lean out.* Not far. Not much. As one might lean out of a doorway to see a caller more clearly. As one might, upon being asked a question of great importance, take a small breath before speaking.

She heard, for the first and last time, the sound of its voice.

It was not a voice. It was the sound the turning had made, only louder, and more slowly, and shaped — very faintly, very clearly — into a single word.

The word was her name.

—

Her mother, when she came in the morning, found the flat unlocked and the lights on and the bathroom door open and the mirror clean and no one at all inside.

There was, on the bathroom floor, a single small dark thing, no bigger than a fingernail clipping.

It was a spiral.

Her mother knelt and looked at it for a long time. Her mother did not touch it.

After a long while her mother stood up. Her mother went into the kitchen. Her mother sat at the kitchen table where her daughter had sat, and her mother placed her palms flat on the wood, and her mother closed her eyes, and her mother listened.

She heard, very faintly, coming from some depth she could not have named, at the very edge of her hearing, the slow patient turning.

Her mother sat at the table for a long time.

She did not, in the end, open her eyes.
